verdicts.claim: SQLite autocheckpoints by default. A checkpoint runs when a COMMIT leaves the WAL at 1000 pages or more, and when the last connection
verdicts.evidence: wal.html 3.1: "automatically checkpoint whenever a COMMIT occurs that causes the WAL file to be 1000 pages or more in size, or when the last database connection on a database file closes"; SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT named in 2.1

verdicts.claim: A checkpoint cannot copy past the end mark of any active reader... also cannot reset the WAL while any reader uses it
verdicts.evidence: wal.html 2.2: "checkpoint must stop when it reaches a page in the WAL that is past the end mark of any current reader"; sec 6: "cannot reset the WAL file because doing so might delete content out from under the reader"

verdicts.claim: journal_size_limit defaults to -1 (no limit). When set, SQLite cuts an oversized WAL down to the limit at each commit or WAL reset; 0 = minimum
verdicts.evidence: pragma.html: "The default journal size limit is -1 (no limit)"; "Each time a transaction is committed or a WAL file resets ... truncated to the limit"; "set the journal_size_limit to zero"

verdicts.claim: TRUNCATE is RESTART plus truncating the WAL file to zero bytes before it reports success
verdicts.evidence: c3ref: "works the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART with the addition that it also truncates the log file to zero bytes just prior to a successful return"

verdicts.claim: NOOP mode checkpoints zero frames. Use PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(NOOP) or SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_NOOP to read pnLog and pnCkpt
verdicts.evidence: c3ref: "This mode always checkpoints zero frames. The only reason to invoke a NOOP checkpoint is to access the values returned ... via *pnLog and *pnCkpt"

verdicts.claim: PRAGMA wal_checkpoint returns one row of three integers. The first is 1 when the equivalent call would return SQLITE_BUSY...
verdicts.evidence: pragma.html: "returns a single row with three integer columns"; col1 1 if equivalent call "would have returned SQLITE_BUSY"; cols 2,3 "-1 if there is no write-ahead log"

verdicts.claim: The WAL-reset bug ... likely affects every release from 3.7.0 (2010-07-21) through 3.51.2 (2026-01-09). Fixed in 3.51.3 (2026-03-13)
verdicts.evidence: wal.html 11: "likely present in all version of SQLite from 3.7.0 (2010-07-21) through 3.51.2 (2026-01-09). It is fixed in version 3.51.3 (2026-03-13) and later. Backports ... 3.44.6 and 3.50.7" (release log itself lists only the fix + date)

verdicts.claim: SQLite 3.52.0 is withdrawn. Its release log says so and moves its planned features to 3.53.0. Tailscale says the fix first shipped in 3.52.0
verdicts.evidence: 3_52_0: marked "Withdrawn"; "features ... originally scheduled for the 3.52.0 release have been moved forward into version 3.53.0"; Tailscale: 3.51.3 "only contained a fix for the WAL-Reset bug"

verdicts.claim: Litestream takes over checkpointing. It starts a long-running read transaction so that no other process can checkpoint and restart the WAL
verdicts.evidence: how-it-works: "It starts a long-running read transaction to prevent any other process from checkpointing and restarting the WAL file"

verdicts.claim: SQLite's developers at first could not reproduce it organically ... Tailscale says the lack of reliable trigger conditions meant it could not reproduce
verdicts.evidence: wal.html 11.2: "The developers were unable to reproduce the bug organically in the lab"; Tailscale: "This lack of reliable trigger conditions meant we couldn't reproduce the bug synthetically"
